Background (from the session that started this one):
JusPrin (repo /Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin, branch jusprin-newui) is an OrcaSlicer fork with an AI Agent pane rendered by a React page (src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI) that talks to native code through a JSON bridge. On 2026-10-20 an "All settings" panel was built in the Agent pane, read-only: it lists every setting in force (process, printer, each filament slot, plate's own settings, each object's customizations), follows the 3D view's selection, and is opened from the setup card's "All settings" link. Its design is the "JusPrin v2" Claude canvas artifact https://claude.ai/artifact/VCEppdwfT7v32W4beUxL1v, page "Current Setup Card", board project/setup-card-all-settings-object.dc.html (read it with the Artifact tool, action read, that path). Kenneth decided the first version ships read-only and the two actions the object board draws come as a follow-up. That work lives on branch claude/sharp-snyder-2d935e (worktree .claude/worktrees/sharp-snyder-2d935e), uncommitted when this brief was written, on top of jusprin-newui 67de3ba99b. Rules: read agent-docs/jusprin/README.md, design-system.md ("Writing UI code") and fork-stewardship.md before touching files outside src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/; every size and colour comes from resources/jusprin/ui/design-tokens.json; guard tests must be shown failing first (restore from a saved copy, never git checkout); no live AI model calls; commit only when Kenneth asks; ask through OrcaSlicer's MessageDialog, never wxMessageBox.

Task:
Add the two edit actions to the All settings panel's object view, as the design board draws them: "Use project value" (Button/Link) under an object's, part's, modifier's or height range's own setting, which removes that key from its config so the project's value applies again; and "Remove" under a support blocker or enforcer row, which deletes that volume. Both are one OrcaSlicer undo step with a readable snapshot name, and each writes a change-log entry the way the agent's edits do (kind "step", actor "person"), so the setup card's "N objects with overrides" note and the panel's rows update from the host.

Where: the page is src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI/src/components/AllSettings.tsx (object view, `objectBody`; the rows are read-only today and the test "one object > lists only what the object sets itself" asserts no action buttons, which must change). Send a new page message (for example `settings_action` with {action, objectId, target, key}) through the bridge: add it to resources/jusprin/agent/protocol.json, Agent/AgentProtocol.hpp and the protocol tests in tests/agent/test_agent_bridge.cpp and AgentUI/src/bridge/protocol.test.ts, and advertise it as a capability (not a protocol version bump). The host side: a new IWorkspace method implemented in src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Workspace/OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp, next to apply_settings (object scope) and the existing object-removal paths, with the fake in tests/jusprin_support/FakeWorkspace.hpp. Dispatch it in Agent/AgentHost.cpp beside handle_settings_catalog. The settings_catalog is re-requested on every context revision, so after the action the panel refreshes itself.

Done means: the two links show only in the object view and only on rows they apply to; pressing one changes the project in the running app (prove it with the shell harness, tests/shell/shell_harness.cpp, whose --setup-differences-capture mode already opens the panel and chooses "Whole project" through the Select; add a step that opens the object, uses the action and checks the row goes and Orca's undo brings it back); unit tests on both sides, with guard tests shown failing first; AgentUI `npm test`, the agent_bridge_tests target and the harness run green. Do not add any other editing, and do not name setting keys in AllSettings.tsx (an acceptance guard forbids all but `extruder`).

name: jusprin-worktree-build
description: How to configure a JusPrin worktree build reusing existing deps; BUILD_TESTS=ON needed for tests
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: reference
  originSessionId: 01c34c35-1546-40fb-a600-c49b2e1ffa06
  modified: 2026-09-18T23:36:14.653Z
---

A JusPrin git worktree builds against the already-built deps by configuring:

```
cmake -B build/arm64 -G "Ninja Multi-Config" -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DCMAKE_OSX_ARCHITECTURES=arm64 -DCMAKE_OSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET=15.0 \
  -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH="/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/deps/build/arm64/OrcaSlicer_dep/usr/local;/Users/kenneth/Projects/OrcaSlicer/deps/build/arm64/OrcaSlicer_dep/usr/local" \
  -DSLIC3R_GUI=ON -DSLIC3R_STATIC=ON -DSLIC3R_PCH=ON -DBUILD_TESTS=ON \
  -DCMAKE_AR=/opt/homebrew/opt/llvm/bin/llvm-ar -DCMAKE_RANLIB=/opt/homebrew/opt/llvm/bin/llvm-ranlib
```

CMAKE BINARY (2026-09-29): configure with `/Applications/CMake.app/Contents/bin/cmake` (put it first on PATH). Homebrew's cmake 4.1 at /opt/homebrew/bin fails with "Could NOT find Eigen3 (missing: EIGEN3_VERSION_OK) (Required is at least version 5.0.1)", and a failed configure poisons the cache: `rm -rf build` before retrying.

The two `CMAKE_AR`/`CMAKE_RANLIB` flags are required on a FRESH build dir:
without them Apple's ar is used and liblibslic3r_gui.a (>4 GiB in
RelWithDebInfo) fails to archive. They only work at first configure, not on
reconfigure. Full story: agent-docs/macos-build-troubleshooting.md. See
[[liblibslic3r-gui-4gib-ar-limit]].

FRESH WORKTREE TRAP (2026-09-18): building only `shell_integration_harness`
does not build the web pages. Also build `--target jusprin_web jusprin_catalogs`
(needs node on PATH: /Users/kenneth/.nvm/versions/node/v24.13.0/bin). Without
them resources/jusprin/{home,agent}/index.html are missing, no web views are
created, and the harness silently tests something else (printer panel starts
shown; web-view crashes vanish).

`BUILD_TESTS=ON` is required or the tests/ tree (workspace, shell targets) is
not generated. Build with `cmake --build build/arm64 --config RelWithDebInfo
--target <targets>`. wxWidgets 3.3 sources for API verification live under
/Users/kenneth/Projects/OrcaSlicer/deps/build/arm64/dep_wxWidgets-prefix/.

CWD TRAP (cost real time once): the harness resets the Bash cwd to the main
repo /Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin between turns, so a *relative*
`cmake --build build/arm64` silently builds the MAIN repo's build dir, not the
worktree's — the worktree binary then runs stale code and a re-fix looks like it
"didn't take". Always pass the worktree build dir as an ABSOLUTE path to
`cmake --build /…/.claude/worktrees/<wt>/build/arm64 …`, and run test binaries by
absolute path. Also: `cmake --build --target <one_exe>` may relink against a
stale lib without recompiling a changed .cpp in that lib — build the app target
(e.g. OrcaSlicer) too so the lib recompiles; verify with
`grep -c '<file>.cpp.o' build.log`. Editing tools (Edit/Write) use absolute
paths so source edits land correctly regardless of cwd.

STALE PROMPT TRAP (2026-09-23): `--target shell_integration_harness` does NOT
rebuild the web pages, so a harness run after an edit to AgentUI (for example
printerInstructions.ts) loads the old bundle. Six --printer-live runs were
wasted this way. After any page edit, build `jusprin_web` explicitly and check
the new text is in resources/jusprin/agent/index.html before running live.

DISK (2026-10-10): building with `--config Release` instead of RelWithDebInfo made a fresh worktree build dir 859 MB instead of ~14 GB, needed no llvm-ar relink, and the shell harness ran normally from `tests/shell/Release/`. Use it when the disk is nearly full (it was at 99%) and no debugger is needed. With other sessions building, a fresh build took far longer than usual (machine load 30 to 85).

name: never-reuse-another-sessions-worktree
description: "A clean, merged, idle worktree under .claude/worktrees still belongs to its session; its owner can resume and check out over you mid-run. Always create your own."
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: cb4c8804-b0a0-4ca0-b4a5-6b6998947d4b
  modified: 2026-09-24T00:36:34.672Z
---

On 2026-09-23 I reused `.claude/worktrees/compassionate-gould-f98259` to skip a full build: it was clean, detached at a commit already merged into jusprin-newui, no process had files open there, and its build dir was only 9 days old. An hour later its owning session resumed, checked out two other branches there (the reflog shows it), rewrote ~13,800 resource files, and my running harness crashed with "Could not load bitmap: bed_high_templ" -- a symptom that looked like a product bug.

**Why:** "clean and idle" says nothing about ownership. The session that created a worktree can resume at any time, and it has no way to know someone else moved in.

**How to apply:** create a new worktree with its own name (`git worktree add -b <branch> .claude/worktrees/<name> <base>`) and configure a fresh build dir with the flags in [[jusprin-worktree-build]]. At jusprin-newui bd8ea51abc a fresh build of `jusprin_web jusprin_catalogs agent_bridge_tests shell_integration_harness` was 881 ninja steps, not the hour I feared. If a harness run dies strangely, check `git -C <worktree> reflog -3 --date=iso` and file mtimes before suspecting the code. Related: [[subagent-worktrees-create-manually]].

name: bash-cwd-resets-after-background
description: "The Bash tool's working directory silently reverts to the primary repo after a run_in_background command or a failed cd; worktree commands must cd explicitly or use absolute paths."
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: 3bfe66db-4c50-4102-b9b3-5ec3eab0060d
  modified: 2026-09-02T18:12:49.419Z
---

While working in a git worktree, a later `cmake --build build/arm64` and a
`git status` ran in `/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin` (the main checkout)
instead of the worktree, so one build reported "no work to do" and a status
check looked as if every edit had been lost.

**Why:** After a `run_in_background` Bash call, and after a compound command
whose `cd` failed, the session cwd is the primary working directory again.
The tool result even says so, but it is easy to miss in a long session.

**How to apply:** In worktree sessions start every Bash command with
`cd <worktree> &&`, or use absolute paths everywhere (python patch scripts
with an absolute root are safest). Verify with `pwd` before trusting a
`git status` that looks wrong. See [[jusprin-worktree-build]].

name: background-bash-timeout-kills-builds
description: "A run_in_background Bash build dies at the tool timeout (ninja prints \"interrupted by user\", exit 130); launch long builds with nohup and watch the log instead"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: 8c1e8dd3-1475-48e9-9398-2d5eaa424bab
  modified: 2026-09-14T19:01:34.576Z
---

A `cmake --build` started with the Bash tool's `run_in_background` is still
bound by that call's `timeout` (default 120 s, max 600 s). When it fires the
build log ends with `ninja: build stopped: interrupted by user.` and `exit=130`,
which looks like a human Ctrl-C but is the harness. Seen 2026-09-14 on a
725-step JusPrin rebuild.

**Why:** the notification says "completed" and the log shows no compiler
error, so it is easy to misread as a finished build; the changed files had not
compiled at all.

**How to apply:** for anything longer than a few minutes, start it detached
(`nohup sh -c "cmake --build … > log 2>&1; echo exit=\$? >> log" & disown`),
then arm a Monitor on the log that reports progress and the `exit=` line. Check
`grep -c '<file>.cpp.o' log` before trusting the result. Related:
[[track-wall-clock-on-background-work]], [[jusprin-worktree-build]].

name: liblibslic3r-gui-4gib-ar-limit
description: "RelWithDebInfo liblibslic3r_gui.a crossed Apple ar's 4 GiB archive limit on jusprin-newui (2026-09-13); CMAKE_AR override is ignored; manual llvm-ar relink recipe and its cd trap"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: 0771473f-5d46-4419-b8e5-112938ea6b34
  modified: 2026-09-14T14:18:50.456Z
---

On 2026-09-13, at jusprin-newui 770bd2b0a2 (after "Add the evidence-led Add a
printer flow"), a worktree RelWithDebInfo build failed archiving
`src/slic3r/RelWithDebInfo/liblibslic3r_gui.a`:
`Assertion failed: (memberOffset < 0xFFFFFFFF) ... ArchiveWriter.cpp` then
`fatal error in .../ranlib`. The archive llvm-ar produced was 4,309,350,176
bytes; the main checkout's copy built minutes earlier was 4,143,827,796 and
still fit. Objects are big because the root CMakeLists.txt (lines ~544-548)
rewrites RelWithDebInfo -O2 to -O0 on purpose. Disk space was not the cause.

**Why:** the failed build left the OLD harness binary in place, and the harness
runs afterwards "passed" against stale code (a new `--printer-setup` flag
silently ran the default mode: same 285 check count). Gate runs on build
success and compare binary mtime.

**How to apply:**
- `-DCMAKE_AR=/opt/homebrew/opt/llvm/bin/llvm-ar` on an existing build dir does
  nothing: `CMakeFiles/<ver>/CMakeCXXCompiler.cmake` sets CMAKE_AR as a normal
  variable that shadows the cache.
- Working relink: `ninja -f build-RelWithDebInfo.ninja -t commands <target>`,
  drop compile lines, swap ar/ranlib for llvm-ar/llvm-ranlib on the gui archive
  line only, then run EACH line in its own `(cd build/arm64 && eval "$line")`.
  One `sh` script fails with bogus "no such file" errors because the
  encoding-check line does `cd src/slic3r` and it leaks; `sh -e` also does not
  stop inside `&&` chains. Apple's linker accepted the >4 GiB llvm-ar archive.
- The fix is PER BUILD DIRECTORY, nothing in the repo selects llvm-ar. Main
  checkout's build/arm64 cache has llvm-ar (commit 449b676145 documents it in
  agent-docs/macos-build-troubleshooting.md); any newly configured build dir
  gets Apple ar and fails again. Configure new dirs with the flags in
  [[jusprin-worktree-build]].
- Recurred 2026-09-14 on a fresh worktree at jusprin-newui bc19661a7f (archive
  4,308,513,464 bytes). Shortcut that worked: after the failed build, from
  `-t commands shell_integration_harness` drop lines containing ` -c `; only
  the last two remain relevant (gui archive, then harness link). Run just
  those two, swapping ar/ranlib on the archive line. Harness then passed.
- A lasting fix (llvm-ar in the toolchain, thin archives, or less debug info)
  is Kenneth's call; the main checkout will hit this on its next growth.

Related: [[jusprin-worktree-build]], [[track-wall-clock-on-background-work]].

Found 2026-09-17 while fixing the journey-tools branch (merged to jusprin-newui as 35eb1b4a59).

`tests/workspace/real_adapter_harness.cpp` does its work in one synchronous run. On macOS, Orca adds each web view's script handler from a CallAfter (`src/slic3r/GUI/Widgets/WebView.cpp`) that runs a script and waits on the page in a nested event loop. In this harness the first one never returns, so `is_adding_script_handler()` stays true, the later views pile up in the static `g_delay_webviews`, and `post_init` (gated on that flag in `GUI_App.cpp`) never runs, even if the harness waits for it (it times out at 180 s).

Closing the main frame ends that wait; the deferred view setup (use-after-free on destroyed views) and then `post_init` (on a destroyed frame) run and segfault (exit 139) after `HARNESS RESULT PASS`. The harness therefore closes the frame only when `post_initialized()` (true on Windows, where the handler is added synchronously) and otherwise calls `ExitMainLoop()`.

**Why:** a Windows fix switched the exit to `Close(true)` and made every macOS run crash; an Orca-side fix (drop destroyed views from `g_delay_webviews`) removed only one of the two crashes.

**How to apply:** if the workspace harness crashes on exit, look here first; don't make it wait for post_init. The shell harness is unaffected because its checks are asynchronous. Related: [[orca-inherited-teardown-crash]], [[background-bash-timeout-kills-builds]].

# Fork stewardship

**Status:** Required discipline for every change to an upstream-owned file on `jusprin-newui`.

JusPrin is a long-lived fork. Every line it changes in an OrcaSlicer-owned file is a line it re-resolves at every rebase, forever, by a person who was not there when the line was written. The rules below exist to keep that permanent cost small and, where it cannot be small, to keep it visible.

One question generates all of them: **after this change, what does the fork own?**

- Owning *product policy* is safe. It is ours, upstream will never write it, and it lives in our files.
- Owning a *small neutral seam* is acceptable. It is the kind of thing upstream might plausibly have written itself, so it survives refactors and could be contributed back.
- Owning *upstream's behavior* is the expensive kind. It commits us to re-deriving upstream's intent forever, and the day we take ownership is usually the day the behavior quietly diverges.

Two mechanical facts drive everything else. Git merges text, not meaning: it conflicts when two sides touch the same or adjacent lines, and it stays silent when they touch different lines even if the result is nonsense. And a conflict is a *stop* — a human is forced to look — while silent divergence is unbounded and invisible. Conflicts are therefore not the enemy. Unnoticed drift is, and conflicts that resolve wrongly are.

## The ten principles

### 1. Conflict probability is about where you write, not how much

**Rule.** Place fork edits where upstream rarely writes, and keep the number of distinct sites low.

**Mechanism.** Risk is roughly *how often upstream edits this region* times *how much of the region you occupy*, summed over every place you touched. Each site is an independent draw. New files have probability zero, so their size is free; one line inside a function upstream is actively reworking is expensive.

**The test.** How many separate places does this change touch, and how busy is each one? Would one seam deliver the same capability?

**Violation.** Delivering a single capability through a dozen scattered notification lines across several upstream files, when one funnel that every path already passes through would have carried them.

### 2. A clean merge is not a safe merge

**Rule.** Prefer edits that are locally correct over edits that participate in upstream's control flow.

**Mechanism.** Git merges text. If your edit's correctness depends on the code around it — an ordering, a guard, an early return, an invariant nobody wrote down — upstream can restructure the surroundings, the merge succeeds, and your edit now runs under assumptions that no longer hold, with no signal at all.

**The test.** If upstream restructures the code around this hunk, do I get a conflict or silence? If silence, would any test catch it?

**Violation.** Moving a member out of a constructor's initializer list because a callback can fire mid-construction. Nothing in upstream's code records that invariant, so a future cleanup restores the old form with no conflict and no error.

### 3. Add to upstream's code; do not revise it

**Rule.** Append, insert, and call. Do not rewrite upstream functions or change their signatures.

**Mechanism.** An additive hook fails gracefully: when it conflicts, the resolution is "keep both," and anyone can do that correctly. A rewritten function fails badly: every future upstream change to it is a conflict whose resolution requires re-deriving two intents at once, in code no longer shared with upstream. Rewriting subtle logic also tends to change it, and you find out later.

**The test.** Does upstream's line survive my change? If I deleted or replaced one, why could I not have added next to it?

**Violation.** Replacing OrcaSlicer's undo and redo implementations with fork-owned equivalents in order to learn whether the history position moved. Re-expressing the vendor-specific snapshot walk silently dropped one of its branches. An additive helper that reports the result, leaving upstream's functions untouched, would have answered the same question.

### 4. Own the policy; borrow the mechanism

**Rule.** No product name, color, dimension, or product-specific decision in an upstream-owned file. Upstream files may gain small neutral capabilities; the policy that uses them lives in fork-owned code.

**Mechanism.** Product specifics in upstream files are permanent divergence: they can never be upstreamed and never dropped, so they must be re-resolved forever. A neutral capability — a flag, a getter/setter pair, an event — reads like something upstream could have written, which is exactly why it survives refactors.

**The test.** Would this addition look reasonable in an upstream pull request, with no explanation of our product?

**Violation.** A product-named enum value inside a rendering class, or product decisions embedded in an upstream mouse handler. The fix is a neutral options struct plus a fork-owned controller that applies our policy.

### 5. One seam beats many touch points

**Rule.** Find the single place every path already passes through, and put the fork's line there.

**Mechanism.** Each touch point is an independent conflict draw and an independent thing a future resolver must understand. Collapsing many small recurring costs into one is worth some indirection.

**The test.** Do all the paths I am hooking already converge somewhere downstream? Is there one function that runs exactly when the thing I care about has happened?

**Violation.** Publishing a history-changed event from undo, from redo, and from both history-navigation entry points, when all four funnel through a single update function that runs only on a successful move.

### 6. One shared implementation is worth a guaranteed conflict

**Rule.** When the alternative is two copies of the same behavior, keep the shared path and accept that it will conflict.

**Mechanism.** A conflict is a stop; drift between two copies is silent and unbounded. Trading an invisible risk for a visible, small, recurring one is a good trade.

**The test.** Where did the logic I removed actually go? A move has one implementation; only a duplication risks divergence. If I wrote new behavior beside an existing upstream path rather than calling it, upstream's future improvements will never reach our users.

**Violation.** Writing a second object-duplication routine next to OrcaSlicer's clipboard path and pointing an existing dialog at it. Reusing the existing path — extending it where it was too narrow — keeps one implementation.

### 7. Unavoidable conflicts must be easy to resolve correctly

**Rule.** When you must delete or relocate an upstream line, say at the site what moved, where it went, and what a future rebase must carry across.

**Mechanism.** The real cost of a conflict is not the stop; it is the chance of resolving it wrongly. Appending near an upstream line yields a conflict whose obvious resolution — keep both — is right. Deleting an upstream line yields a conflict whose obvious resolution — take mine, the logic moved — silently discards whatever upstream did to that line in the meantime.

**The test.** Six months from now, is the natural resolution of the conflict I am creating the correct one? If not, what does the resolver need to read to get it right, and is that text next to the conflict?

**Violation.** Removing an upstream snapshot label that upstream later localized. Git stops for a human, but the intent-faithful resolution throws the translation away, and nothing at the site says otherwise.

### 8. Do not diverge where you gain nothing; converge where upstream already went

**Rule.** No gratuitous formatting, reordering, or whitespace differences. Before reverting a cosmetic difference, compare against current upstream — it may have made the same change.

**Mechanism.** Every valueless difference is a conflict site that buys nothing. And if upstream has independently arrived at your version, "fixing" it back creates divergence rather than removing it. Adopting a change upstream has already made converges the two trees early and makes the eventual conflict resolve itself.

**The test.** Does this difference carry meaning? Has upstream already made it?

**Violation.** Consuming a shared blank line in a list of build subdirectories, where upstream also appends entries.

### 9. Verify the risk claim instead of reasoning about it

**Rule.** Before asserting that a change is or is not rebase-risky, check it. Three checks, each one command: does git actually conflict there; has upstream already converged on the same change; is the change a move or a duplication.

**Mechanism.** A coherent story about fork risk is not a true one, and every one of these is cheaper to check than to argue about. Reasoning alone reliably produces confident, wrong claims — that a lost change is "silent" when git stops for it, that a move is a "duplication," that a cosmetic difference is gratuitous when upstream shares it.

**The test.** Did I run the simulation, or am I describing what I expect it to say?

**Violation.** A report that lists which files are rebase-sensitive and calls the change narrow, without having run the merge simulation that would have found two lossy resolutions waiting in it.

### 10. Pull direction dominates every local edit

**Rule.** Replay the fork's own commits onto upstream. Never merge upstream in, and never rebase the whole branch.

**Mechanism.** The fork's own footprint is small; the inherited release-branch history is not. Merging upstream in makes the conflict surface the entire divergence between the release branch and upstream's development line — none of it ours. Rebasing only our commits discards that inherited history by taking upstream's version of every file we never touched.

**The test.** Am I replaying our commits onto upstream, or bringing upstream into ours?

**Violation.** `git merge upstream/main`, which produces a conflict list dominated by vendor profiles, translations, and CI files that JusPrin has never edited.

## Writing UI code

Rules for anyone, human or agent, adding or changing a JusPrin surface. They
exist because every value that is typed by hand drifts from Figma and from
the other side of the app within weeks; today's guards catch most of it, but
only if the code goes through the token file in the first place.

1. **Never type a color, radius, font, or control size.** Every one comes
   from `resources/jusprin/ui/design-tokens.json`. Native code reads it
   through `ShellTheme`: `palette(dark)` for color, `metrics()` for radii,
   spacing, and per-component sizes, `font(role)` for type. A stock
   `wxStaticText`, `wxTextCtrl`, or OrcaSlicer `Button` is
   dressed through `Shell/ShellRecipes.hpp`, never by calling its setters
   with literals. The Agent page uses only `var(--…)`: `--<group>-<name>` for
   color, `--radius-<name>`, `--font-<role>`, `--font-code`, and
   `--button-<recipe>-padding`.
2. **If the value you need has no token, add the token first.** Put it in
   the JSON, extend the guard in `tests/brand/test_brand_tokens.cpp` so a
   later edit cannot silently move it, then read it from code. Do not write
   the number "for now": the guards cannot see a literal that is already
   there, and the next reader cannot tell a decision from an accident. A
   value that exists in Figma but not in the roles or scales is a design
   decision to raise, not a reason to type it.
3. **Layout spacing may stay literal, on the scale.** Padding between
   regions, gaps, and margins use 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 32, 40, or 48 DIP.
   Control padding is not layout spacing; it comes from a button recipe.
4. **Pick the nearest role, never a bespoke size.** The roles are the whole
   type system. Bold at a body or label size is a role of its own; if a
   surface seems to need a size that no role has, see rule 2.
5. **The design system wins when it and the code disagree.** The two Claude
   artifacts are the source of truth (Kenneth, 2026-10-20; Figma is
   retired): the Design System
   (https://claude.ai/artifact/3zgiix8rAw3rXextQnR5UL) and the "JusPrin v2"
   canvas (https://claude.ai/artifact/VCEppdwfT7v32W4beUxL1v). Change the
   token file to match, or, when the code's value is the one to keep, change
   the artifact first. Do not trust old commit messages about either.
6. **Run the guards before calling UI work done:** `brand_tokens_tests`,
   `shell_theme_tests`, and `npm test` in `AgentUI`. Then look at the surface
   in the running app; the guards prove the code went through the tokens,
   not that the result looks right.
7. **Upstream files are off limits for style.** OrcaSlicer's own screens are
   retinted through the hooks `BrandPalette.cpp` installs and nothing else;
   see [Fork stewardship](fork-stewardship.md). Their radii and fonts stay

3. [Engineering and verification method](engineering-method.md) — how to assess risk and what evidence is required before calling a feature complete.
4. [OrcaSlicer integration guide](orca-integration-guide.md) — known Orca behaviors, lifecycle traps, event and history constraints, and testing lessons.
5. [Fork stewardship](fork-stewardship.md) — required before changing any OrcaSlicer-owned file: where a seam belongs, why additive beats rewritten, how to leave a conflict that resolves correctly, and what evidence a change must record.
6. [Design system](design-system.md) — brand behavior, semantic UI tokens, typography, spacing, accessibility, and asset rules.

## Governing decisions

- JusPrin is an AI-piloted 3D-printing product built on OrcaSlicer, not a replacement slicing engine.
- OrcaSlicer's C++ model, slicing pipeline, viewport, geometry operations, project serialization, and undo stack remain authoritative.
- The production application stays native C++/wxWidgets/OpenGL. The Agent conversation uses a local React/TypeScript application inside `wxWebView`.
- JavaScript renders state and submits typed commands; it never owns editable Orca project state.
- When logic could live in either C++ or a React page, it goes in the page unless there is a strong reason for C++: it touches Orca state, enforces a limit or boundary the app must guarantee, has to work without a page, or needs a thread or lifetime the page lacks. See [Where logic goes](architecture.md#where-logic-goes-the-page-first).
- Product policy lives in fork-owned files. OrcaSlicer-owned files receive only small, product-neutral, additive seams — every line changed there is a line this fork re-resolves at every rebase.
- The user owns physical facts, object meaning, desired outcomes, privacy and legal decisions, and starting consequential physical actions.
- The production branch must not import experimental POC behavior merely because it demonstrated feasibility. Use the POC as evidence and reimplement through stable production boundaries.

Lessons from driving the printer chat through `--printer-live` with the live model and the fake Bambu printer:

- **A reply's later lines have no `HARNESS LIVE` prefix.** A `Choices:` line sits on its own log line, so `grep "HARNESS LIVE"` hides it. On 2026-09-23 this produced a wrong report that the model never offered choices. Grep `^Choices:` separately.
- **A failed run keeps its data dir, with the API key in it.** The harness prints `HARNESS DATA DIR kept for inspection: /var/folders/.../jusprin-shell-*`. Delete the dir your own run printed, by that path. Do not sweep every `jusprin-shell-*` holding a key: another session may be running the harness in the same checkout, and on 2026-09-23 a sweep deleted a live instance's data dir.
- **Re-selecting the selected Bambu LAN printer deselects it.** DevManager's "same lan machine" path disconnects and reconnects, and GUI_App's local-connect handler (CallAfter) then sees the lost status and calls `set_selected_machine("")` after the reconnect. The connection reports "The selected printer changed". `OrcaPrinterBackend::connect_printer` now deselects and re-selects on the next event turn. The fake printer auto-selects itself when discovered, so the first connect always hits this.
- **Close OrcaSlicer's printer list (GuideFrame) only after its page loads.** It installs its web page's script handler from a CallAfter that waits on the page; `EndModal` before the load leaves that wait hanging on a hidden view, and the app freezes with no window. On 2026-09-23 this was first blamed on the product and "fixed" with a deferral, then traced to the test and reverted. Wait for `!is_adding_script_handler()`, a non-busy page and a URL, as the old `setup_manual` check did.
- **Open the panel through `ShellController::open_printer_conversation`** in live tests; `PrinterPanel::open` skips the full-window layout.
- **The model's reliability is measured, not assumed.** gpt-5.4-mini saved changes without waiting for yes in 6 of 10 runs, even with an explicit "ask, then stop" prompt. Count across several runs before calling prompt wording fixed.

See [[live-test-built-app-on-mac]] and [[fake-bambu-printer-sim]].
